claim: Gap junction channels are formed by two unrelated protein families: innexins and connexins.
source: Gap junction channels are formed by two unrelated protein families. Non-chordates use the primordial innexins, while chordates use connexins that superseded the gap junction function of innexins.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about gap junction protein families, supported by the manuscript's introduction and citations throughout.

claim: Non-chordates use innexins as gap junction proteins.
source: Non-chordates use the primordial innexins, while chordates use connexins that superseded the gap junction function of innexins.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited in the abstract and supported by the literature.

claim: Chordates use connexins that superseded the gap junction function of innexins.
source: Non-chordates use the primordial innexins, while chordates use connexins that superseded the gap junction function of innexins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about chordate gap junction proteins.

claim: Chordates retained innexin-homologs, but N-glycosylation prevents them from forming gap junctions.
source: Chordates retained innexin-homologs, but N-glycosylation prevents them from forming gap junctions.
evidence: This is supported by citations and experimental evidence discussed in the manuscript.

claim: The study identified glycosylation sites of 2388 innexins from 174 non-chordate and 276 chordate species.
source: Here, we identified glycosylation sites of 2388 innexins from 174 non-chordate and 276 chordate species.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on the data analysis performed in the study.

claim: Not a single innexin without glycosylation sites was found among all chordates.
source: Among all chordates, we found not a single innexin without glycosylation sites.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the comprehensive analysis of chordate innexins.

claim: The glycosylation motif is widespread among non-chordate innexins.
source: Surprisingly, the glycosylation motif is also widespread among non-chordate innexins indicating that glycosylated innexins are not a novelty of chordates.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the analysis of non-chordate innexins.

claim: Glycosylated innexins are not a novelty of chordates.
source: Surprisingly, the glycosylation motif is also widespread among non-chordate innexins indicating that glycosylated innexins are not a novelty of chordates.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that glycosylation motifs are widespread in non-chordates.

claim: A loss of innexin diversity occurred during early chordate evolution.
source: In addition, we discovered a loss of innexin diversity during early chordate evolution.
evidence: This is a primary finding from comparing innexin diversity across taxa.

claim: Lancelets lack connexins.
source: Most importantly, lancelets, which lack connexins, exclusively possess only one highly conserved innexin with one glycosylation site.
evidence: This is based on database searches and analysis of lancelet genomes and transcriptomes.

claim: Lancelets exclusively possess only one highly conserved innexin with one glycosylation site.
source: Most importantly, lancelets, which lack connexins, exclusively possess only one highly conserved innexin with one glycosylation site.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the analysis of lancelet innexins.

claim: A bottleneck effect might explain why connexins have become the only protein used to form chordate gap junctions.
source: A bottleneck effect might thus explain why connexins have become the only protein used to form chordate gap junctions.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the findings about innexin diversity loss.

claim: Innexins have been identified in all eumetazoans except sponges, placozoa, and echinoderms.
source: The innexins are the primordial gap junction proteins that have been identified in all eumetazoans except sponges, placozoa, and echinoderms (Slivko-Koltchik et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Connexins arose de novo during early chordate evolution.
source: The connexins arose de novo during the early chordate evolution and constitute the gap junction channels of all living chordates except lancelets (Abascal and Zardoya, 2013; Mikalsen et al., 2021; Slivko-Koltchik et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Connexins constitute the gap junction channels of all living chordates except lancelets.
source: The connexins arose de novo during the early chordate evolution and constitute the gap junction channels of all living chordates except lancelets (Abascal and Zardoya, 2013; Mikalsen et al., 2021; Slivko-Koltchik et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Each hemichannel is composed of six connexins or eight innexins.
source: Each hemichannel is composed of six connexins or eight innexins, respectively (Skerrett and Williams, 2017).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Connexins and innexins are encoded by large gene families.
source: As connexins and innexins are encoded by large gene families (Mikalsen et al., 2021; Yen and Saier, 2007), different connexin- and innexin-based gap junction channels can be formed to fulfill unique functions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Connexins and innexins lack sequence homology.
source: Despite the lack of sequence homology (Alexopoulos et al., 2004), the topology (Maeda et al., 2009; Michalski et al., 2020; Oshima et al., 2016; Figure 1A and B) and function (Pereda and Macagno, 2017; Skerrett and Williams, 2017) of connexin- and innexin-based gap junction channels are remarkably similar.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The topology of connexin- and innexin-based gap junction channels are remarkably similar.
source: Despite the lack of sequence homology (Alexopoulos et al., 2004), the topology (Maeda et al., 2009; Michalski et al., 2020; Oshima et al., 2016; Figure 1A and B) and function (Pereda and Macagno, 2017; Skerrett and Williams, 2017) of connexin- and innexin-based gap junction channels are remarkably similar.
evidence: This is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1A and B.

claim: The function of connexin- and innexin-based gap junction channels are remarkably similar.
source: Despite the lack of sequence homology (Alexopoulos et al., 2004), the topology (Maeda et al., 2009; Michalski et al., 2020; Oshima et al., 2016; Figure 1A and B) and function (Pereda and Macagno, 2017; Skerrett and Williams, 2017) of connexin- and innexin-based gap junction channels are remarkably similar.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Vertebrates express innexin-homologs called pannexins.
source: Vertebrates still express innexin-homologs (Baranova et al., 2004; Panchin et al., 2000), called pannexins, but it is supposed that these stopped forming gap junctions and since then only function as non-junctional membrane channels (Dahl and Muller, 2014; Esseltine and Laird, 2016; Sosinsky et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Pannexins are supposed to have stopped forming gap junctions and only function as non-junctional membrane channels.
source: Vertebrates still express innexin-homologs (Baranova et al., 2004; Panchin et al., 2000), called pannexins, but it is supposed that these stopped forming gap junctions and since then only function as non-junctional membrane channels (Dahl and Muller, 2014; Esseltine and Laird, 2016; Sosinsky et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The three pannexins of humans and mice are glycoproteins.
source: This hypothesis is based on the discovery that the three pannexins of humans and mice are glycoproteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge based on experimental evidence cited in the manuscript.

claim: Each human and mouse pannexin contains an identified consensus motif (Asn-X-Ser/Thr) for asparagine (N)-linked glycosylation within either the first or the second extracellular loop.
source: Each of the pannexins contains an identified consensus motif (Asn-X-Ser/Thr) for asparagine (N)-linked glycosylation within either the first or the second extracellular loop (EL; Penuela et al., 2007; Penuela et al., 2014a; Ruan et al., 2020; Sanchez-Pupo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: N-linked glycosylation enables the posttranslational attachment of sugar moieties at the asparagine residue within the consensus sequence which hinders two pannexin channels of adjacent cells to form intercellular channels.
source: This enables the posttranslational attachment of sugar moieties at the asparagine residue within the consensus sequence which hinders two pannexin channels of adjacent cells to form intercellular channels (Ruan et al., 2020; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: Aedes aegypti possesses an innexin protein with an extracellular NGS that is glycosylated.
source: Specifically, previous studies have shown that at least two non-chordate species, Aedes aegypti (Calkins et al., 2015) and Caenorhabditis elegans (Kaji et al., 2007), possess an innexin protein with an extracellular NGS that is glycosylated.
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental work.

claim: Caenorhabditis elegans possesses an innexin protein with an extracellular NGS that is glycosylated.
source: Specifically, previous studies have shown that at least two non-chordate species, Aedes aegypti (Calkins et al., 2015) and Caenorhabditis elegans (Kaji et al., 2007), possess an innexin protein with an extracellular NGS that is glycosylated.
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental work.

claim: Putative NGS have been described in a terrestrial slug (Limax valentianus).
source: Additionally, putative NGS have also been described in a terrestrial slug (Limax valentianus) (Sadamoto et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The study collected amino acid sequences of 1521 non-chordate innexins from 174 species across nine higher-level taxonomic groups.
source: In total, we collected the amino acid sequences of 1521 non-chordate innexins from 174 species across nine higher-level taxonomic groups (ctenophores, cnidarians, molluscs, annelids, platyhelminthes, nematodes, arthropods, xenacoelomorphs, and echinoderms).
evidence: This describes the data collection methodology and results.

claim: 67% of ctenophore innexins have extracellular NGSs.
source: Surprisingly, we found that innexins with extracellular NGSs are widespread among the examined non-chordate phyla, comprising 67% of the innexins in the ctenophores (Figure 1D and E, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the data analysis, shown in figures.

claim: Innexins with extracellular NGSs are widespread among the examined non-chordate phyla.
source: Surprisingly, we found that innexins with extracellular NGSs are widespread among the examined non-chordate phyla, comprising 67% of the innexins in the ctenophores (Figure 1D and E, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the data analysis.

claim: The position of the NGSs within the ELs as well as the residues around the N-glycosylation consensus motifs are not conserved between the phyla.
source: The position of the NGSs within the ELs as well as the residues around the N-glycosylation consensus motifs are not conserved between the phyla (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a finding from sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: No extracellular NGS was found that was conserved in all species within a phylum.
source: However, we did not find any extracellular NGS that was conserved in all species within a phylum.
evidence: This is a finding from the comparative analysis of innexins.

claim: Innexins originated early in metazoan evolution and have undergone diversification within the different non-chordate phyla.
source: As shown in previous studies (Abascal and Zardoya, 2013; Hasegawa and Turnbull, 2014; Moroz et al., 2014), and demonstrated in Figure 1D, innexins originated early in metazoan evolution and have undergone diversification within the different non-chordate phyla.
evidence: This is supported by citations and demonstrated in the phylogenetic tree.

claim: Innexins with extracellular NGSs evolved independently numerous times within the single phyla.
source: Thus, innexins with extracellular NGSs evolved independently numerous times within the single phyla.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic analysis and lack of conservation across phyla.

claim: Connexins were clearly absent in all non-chordate species examined.
source: Another point of interest is that connexins were clearly absent in all species.
evidence: This is a finding from database searches.

claim: A connexin appears evident in the transcriptome of the red sea urchin (Mesocentrotus franciscanus) but is absent in the genomic data.
source: But there is one apparent exception, the red sea urchin (Mesocentrotus franciscanus). Here, a connexin (GenBank accession number GHJZ01010392.1) appears evident in the transcriptome (Wong et al., 2019) but is absent in the genomic data (Sergiev et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on database searches and comparison of transcriptome and genome data.

claim: The putative connexin is clearly absent in any of the 41 available transcriptomes of other echinoderm species, including close relatives.
source: Moreover, the putative connexin is clearly absent in any of the 41 available transcriptomes of other echinoderm species, including close relatives (Strongylocentrotus purpuratus and Hemicentrotus pulcherrimus).
evidence: This is a finding from database searches across multiple echinoderm species.

claim: The identification of innexins in ambulacrarian transcriptomes provides a solution to the paradox of how ambulacrarians form gap junctions.
source: Notably, our survey also solved an old paradox in the ambulacrarians that form gap junctions (as identified by electron microscopy and voltage-clamp experiments) (Andreuccetti et al., 1987; Slivko-Koltchik et al., 2019; Yazaki et al., 1999) but were assumed to lack both innexins and connexins (Abascal and Zardoya, 2013; Burke et al., 2006; Slivko-Koltchik et al., 2019), causing speculations on the nature of their junctions. Our identification of innexins in ambulacrarian transcriptomes (Figure 1D–F and Figure 1—source data 1) provides a simple solution of this puzzle.
evidence: This is a finding from the study that resolves a previously unexplained observation.

claim: A large fraction of non-chordate innexins are likely glycoproteins.
source: The wide occurrence of innexins with NGSs in all non-chordate phyla (Figure 1D and E) as well as the experimentally confirmed NGSs (Calkins et al., 2015; Kaji et al., 2007) strongly suggest that a large fraction of non-chordate innexins are glycoproteins.
evidence: This is inferred from the widespread occurrence of NGSs and experimental confirmation in some species.

claim: Glycosylated innexin channels might not be able to form gap junction channels but rather function as non-junctional channels.
source: These glycosylated innexin channels might then also not be able to form gap junction channels but rather function as non-junctional channels.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the known effect of glycosylation on pannexins.

claim: Seven innexins with identified NGSs have previously been shown to be parts of functional gap junction channels.
source: It is interesting to note that seven of the innexins with identified NGSs have previously been shown to be parts of functional gap junction channels (Figure 1F, Figure 1—source data 3).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous experimental studies.

claim: Non-chordate animals possess a vast diversity of innexins, with and without NGSs.
source: Our findings demonstrate that non-chordate animals possess a vast diversity of innexins, with and without NGSs, and thus presumably function either as non-junctional membrane channels or as intercellular gap junction channels.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the data analysis showing diverse innexins in non-chordates.

claim: The study collected amino acid sequences of 867 chordate innexins from 276 species across nine higher-level taxonomic groups.
source: In total, we collected the amino acid sequences of 867 chordate innexins from 276 species across nine higher-level taxonomic groups (lancelets, tunicates, lampreys, cartilaginous fish, bony fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals) and then searched, as described above, in the ELs of each of the sequences for the consensus motif for N-glycosylation (Asn-X-Ser/Thr).
evidence: This describes the data collection methodology and results for chordates.

claim: Each single innexin in every chordate species has at least one NGS in its ELs.
source: Our results clearly show that each single innexin in every chordate species has at least one NGS in its ELs (Figure 2A and B, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the comprehensive analysis of chordate innexins.

claim: NGS are highly conserved in lancelets, lampreys and across all vertebrate taxa.
source: The NGSs are highly conserved in lancelets, lampreys and across all vertebrate taxa.
evidence: This is a finding from sequence alignment analysis.

claim: NGS were not conserved across the tunicates.
source: NGS were, however, not conserved across the tunicates (Figure 2C–E), which may be consistent with their unusually high amino acid evolutionary rates (Berná and Alvarez-Valin, 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from sequence analysis, with an explanation based on citation.

claim: Across the different vertebrate taxa, the sequences of the ELs as well as the positions of the glycosylation motifs are highly conserved.
source: Across the different vertebrate taxa, the sequences of the ELs as well as the positions of the glycosylation motifs are highly conserved (Figure 2F–H).
evidence: This is a finding from sequence alignment analysis shown in figures.

claim: Conservation of NGS is particularly high in the ELs of Pannexin 2.
source: Among the three pannexins, conservation is particularly high in the ELs of Pannexi 2.
evidence: This is a finding from sequence alignment analysis.

claim: Conservation of NGS is still seen even after the whole-genome duplication in the common ancestor of teleost fishes.
source: Interestingly, conservation is still seen even after the whole-genome duplication in the common ancestor of teleost fishes (Glasauer and Neuhauss, 2014), an event that generally provides a source of genetic raw material for evolutionary innovation and functional divergence.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis with context from citation.

claim: Each single species retained their pannexins with NGSs.
source: Still, each single species retained their pannexins with NGSs (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the comprehensive species analysis.

claim: A single mutation in the N-glycosylation motif might be sufficient to recover the ability of pannexins to form gap junction channels.
source: This is remarkable because a single mutation in the N-glycosylation motif might be sufficient to recover the ability of pannexins to form gap junction channels (Ruan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on citation to experimental work.

claim: The high conservation of the location and surrounding sequences of NGSs strongly suggests that vertebrate innexins serve essential roles.
source: The surprisingly high conservation of the location and the surrounding sequences of NGSs strongly suggests that at least the vertebrate innexins serve essential roles, with correspondingly high stabilizing selective pressures (Abascal and Zardoya, 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from the conservation pattern with support from citation.

claim: N-glycosylation is present in both non-chordate and chordate species.
source: In summary, we show that N-glycosylation is present in both non-chordate and chordate species.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the data analysis.

claim: Simple organisms at the beginning of metazoan evolution attached sugar moieties to some of their innexins to presumably prevent them from forming gap junction channels.
source: Already simple organisms at the beginning of the metazoan evolution attached sugar moieties to some of their innexins to presumably prevent them from forming gap junction channels.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding of glycosylation in early-diverging taxa.

claim: The vertebrate pannexins did not diverge and change their function driven by the appearance of connexins but rather originate from an innexin already equipped with NGS.
source: In consequence, the vertebrate pannexins did not diverge and change their function driven by the appearance of the connexins but rather originate from an innexin already equipped with NGS.
evidence: This is an inference from the evolutionary analysis and finding of widespread glycosylation.

claim: Single membrane channels formed by pannexins and innexins have the same physiological functions and are similar in their biophysical and pharmacological properties.
source: This would be consistent with findings that single membrane channels formed by pannexins and innexins have the same physiological functions and are similar in their biophysical and pharmacological properties (Dahl and Muller, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Chordates are comprised of three subphyla: the lancelets, the tunicates, and the vertebrates.
source: Chordates are comprised of three subphyla: the lancelets, the tunicates, and the vertebrates.
evidence: This is established taxonomic knowledge.

claim: The lancelets represent the most basal chordate lineage that diverged before the split between tunicates and vertebrates.
source: The lancelets represent the most basal chordate lineage that diverged before the split between tunicates and vertebrates (Putnam et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established phylogenetic knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The vertebrates split into the jawless fish (lampreys), the most ancient vertebrate group, and the jawed vertebrates.
source: The vertebrates split into the jawless fish (lampreys), the most ancient vertebrate group (Smith et al., 2018), and the jawed vertebrates (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is established phylogenetic knowledge supported by citation and shown in figure.

claim: The lancelets and the lampreys as well as most of the tunicates have only one innexin.
source: As our previous analysis revealed, the lancelets and the lampreys as well as most of the tunicates have only one innexin.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: In the jawed vertebrates, three innexins (called pannexins) were found in each single species.
source: In the jawed vertebrates, we found three innexins (called pannexins) in each single species.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: The three pannexins in jawed vertebrates resulted from two whole-genome duplications at the early vertebrate lineage leading first to Pannexin-2 and afterward to Pannexin-1 and Pannexin-3.
source: This is expected from the two whole-genome duplications at the early vertebrate lineage leading first to Pannexin-2 and afterward to Pannexin-1 and Pannexin-3 (Abascal and Zardoya, 2013; Fushiki et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Teleost fishes have a fourth pannexin generated by a whole-genome duplication event during the teleost evolution.
source: Only teleost fishes have a fourth pannexin generated by a whole-genome duplication event during the teleost evolution (Bond et al., 2012; Glasauer and Neuhauss, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The limited genetic diversity of innexins in chordates is in strong contrast to the rich innexin diversity within the non-chordate phyla.
source: The limited genetic diversity is thus in strong contrast to the rich innexin diversity within the non-chordate phyla (Figures 1D and 3A; Abascal and Zardoya, 2013; Hasegawa and Turnbull, 2014; Moroz et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing the data across taxa, supported by citations and figures.

claim: Each of the innexins of lancelets, tunicates, and lampreys has an extracellular NGS.
source: Furthermore, we found that each of the innexins of lancelets, tunicates, and lampreys has an extracellular NGS (Figures 2A–E ,–3C).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis shown in figures.

claim: In lancelets the only innexin available contains an NGS in its EL1.
source: Specifically, in lancelets the only innexin available contains an NGS in its EL1.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the lancelet innexin analysis.

claim: Lancelets lost the diversity of innexins but retained one that might not even be capable of forming gap junctions.
source: Hence, lancelets, not only lost the diversity of innexins but retained one that might not even be capable of forming gap junctions.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that the single lancelet innexin has an NGS.

claim: No connexin-like sequences were found in lancelets genomes and transcriptomes.
source: Our work and earlier studies Mikalsen et al., 2021; Slivko-Koltchik et al., 2019 found no connexin-like sequences in lancelets genomes and transcriptomes (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from database searches, consistent with previous studies.

claim: Lancelets could either have no gap junctions at all or one formed from an innexin with an NGS.
source: With connexins absent, lancelets could thus either have no gap junctions at all (see Baatrup, 1981; Lane et al., 1987; Soledad Ruiz and Anadón, 1989) or one formed from an innexin with an NGS.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the findings, with citations to previous observations.

claim: Connexins arose de novo just at the time of early chordate evolution when innexin diversity was lost.
source: Both options, either the complete absence of regular gap junctions or the loss of all functional diversity among them are highly relevant for the evolution of connexins. These arose de novo just at this time of chordate evolution (Figure 3C) and rapidly developed into diverse gene families (Figure 3B) with up to 22 connexins in mammals and 46 connexins in bony fish (Mikalsen et al., 2021) that again enabled a huge diversity of functionally unique gap junctions.
evidence: This is an inference from the evolutionary timing analysis, supported by figures and citation.

claim: Connexins rapidly developed into diverse gene families with up to 22 connexins in mammals and 46 connexins in bony fish.
source: These arose de novo just at this time of chordate evolution (Figure 3C) and rapidly developed into diverse gene families (Figure 3B) with up to 22 connexins in mammals and 46 connexins in bony fish (Mikalsen et al., 2021) that again enabled a huge diversity of functionally unique gap junctions.
evidence: This is supported by citation and shown in figures.

claim: A bottleneck effect at the origin of chordates might have been crucial for the evolution of the novel connexins.
source: Based on our findings, we thus propose that a bottleneck effect at the origin of chordates might have been crucial for the evolution of the novel connexins (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the findings, illustrated in Figure 3D.

claim: Innexins were recruited as gap junction proteins in the last common ancestor of eumetazoa.
source: In this evolutionary scenario, innexins were recruited as gap junction proteins in the last common ancestor of eumetazoa.
evidence: This is part of the proposed evolutionary scenario based on the findings.

claim: While the innexins functionally diverge in ctenophores, cnidarians, and protostomes, the last common ancestor of the deuterostomes had lost all innexin diversity and thus the capacity to form functionally diverse gap junctions.
source: While the innexins functionally diverge in ctenophores, cnidarians, and protostomes, the last common ancestor of the deuterostomes had lost all innexin diversity and thus the capacity to form functionally diverse gap junctions (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is part of the proposed evolutionary scenario based on the findings.

claim: The strikingly high conservation of NGSs in lancelet, lamprey, and jawed vertebrate innexins suggests that the non-junctional innexin channels already served essential physiological functions in the last common ancestor of chordates.
source: The strikingly high conservation of NGSs in lancelet, lamprey, and jawed vertebrate innexins (Figure 2C–H), their expression in every organ (Penuela et al., 2014a) and their association with a variety of diseases (Esseltine and Laird, 2016; Penuela et al., 2014b) suggest that the non-junctional innexin channels already served essential physiological functions in the last common ancestor of chordates and could not be converted into gap junctions.
evidence: This is inferred from conservation patterns and functional data from citations.

claim: The non-junctional innexin channels could not be converted into gap junctions.
source: The strikingly high conservation of NGSs in lancelet, lamprey, and jawed vertebrate innexins (Figure 2C–H), their expression in every organ (Penuela et al., 2014a) and their association with a variety of diseases (Esseltine and Laird, 2016; Penuela et al., 2014b) suggest that the non-junctional innexin channels already served essential physiological functions in the last common ancestor of chordates and could not be converted into gap junctions.
evidence: This is inferred from the conservation and functional importance of glycosylated innexins.

claim: The loss of diversity in gap junctions is extreme in early chordates, with just one, if any at all, functional gap junction.
source: The loss of diversity in gap junctions is thus extreme, with just one, if any at all, functional gap junction.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis of innexin diversity in early chordates.

claim: The loss of innexin diversity and strict conservation of the one remaining innexin could explain why the connexin family arose de novo and why it became the exclusive gap junction protein in all chordates.
source: This finding and that of the strict conservation of the one remaining innexin could thus explain rather simply why the connexin family arose de novo and why it became the exclusive gap junction protein in all chordates although innexin-based gap junctions would have been fully capable to serve all functions (Baker and Macagno, 2014; Bao et al., 2007; Bhattacharya et al., 2019; Lane et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2016; Phelan and Starich, 2001; Skerrett and Williams, 2017; Welzel and Schuster, 2018; Yaksi and Wilson, 2010) as they do so successfully in the sophisticated nervous systems of invertebrates (Calabrese et al., 2016; Hall, 2017; Kristan et al., 2005; Marder et al., 2005; Otopalik et al., 2019).
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, based on the findings and supported by citations showing innexin capabilities.

claim: Innexin-based gap junctions would have been fully capable to serve all functions as they do in the sophisticated nervous systems of invertebrates.
source: This finding and that of the strict conservation of the one remaining innexin could thus explain rather simply why the connexin family arose de novo and why it became the exclusive gap junction protein in all chordates although innexin-based gap junctions would have been fully capable to serve all functions (Baker and Macagno, 2014; Bao et al., 2007; Bhattacharya et al., 2019; Lane et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2016; Phelan and Starich, 2001; Skerrett and Williams, 2017; Welzel and Schuster, 2018; Yaksi and Wilson, 2010) as they do so successfully in the sophisticated nervous systems of invertebrates (Calabrese et al., 2016; Hall, 2017; Kristan et al., 2005; Marder et al., 2005; Otopalik et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies of invertebrate innexin function.

claim: Innexins and connexins share a common membrane topology with four hydrophobic transmembrane domains linked by one intracellular and two extracellular loops.
source: (A) Innexins and (B) connexins are integral membrane proteins that share a common membrane topology with four hydrophobic transmembrane domains (TM) linked by one intracellular (IL) and two extracellular loops (ELs).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and B and is established structural knowledge.

claim: Connexin and innexin proteins can assemble to form a hemichannel.
source: Connexin and innexin proteins can assemble to form a hemichannel.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1 and is established knowledge.

claim: The hemichannels of two neighboring cells can form intercellular gap junction channels that are stabilized by disulfide bonds between cysteine residues in their ELs.
source: The hemichannels of two neighboring cells can form intercellular gap junction channels that are stabilized by disulfide bonds between cysteine residues in their ELs (Dahl et al., 1991) (yellow circles).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1 and supported by citation.

claim: The attachment of glycans to NGSs block the disulfide bond formation and hence prevents the proper docking of the hemichannels and the formation of pannexin-based gap junctions.
